title: Your own pasture
hook: be islands to yourselves; keep to your own ancestral pasture

segments.voice: Yesterday: Payasi and Kassapa, and your line, the sceptic's parables. Did you answer a doubt with respect? Today we start a discourse that runs across three days, and it opens close to home. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

A quail is pecking in an open field when a hawk drops out of the sky and grabs it. As it's carried off, the quail laments: if only I'd stayed in my own ground, among the clods of the plowed field where my family has always lived, this hawk couldn't have touched me. The hawk, amused, lets it go: go on then, back to your ground, see if it saves you. The quail darts into the clods, and calls out a dare. The hawk dives, and the quail slips behind a clod. The hawk hits the earth. Today: your own pasture.
screen: `A QUAIL IN THE OPEN.` → `IF ONLY I'D STAYED HOME.` → `THE HAWK HITS THE CLOD.`

segments.voice: That quail story comes from the Connected Discourses. It's the best commentary on how the twenty-sixth Long Discourse opens, the Cakkavatti Sihanada, the lion's roar on the wheel-turning king. The Buddha is at Matula in Magadha, and he begins: monks, live as islands to yourselves, as your own refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as your island, the Dhamma as your refuge. Then the image the hawk and quail make vivid: keep to your own pasture, the range of your fathers. Walking there, Mara, the tempter, will get no chance at you. The Pali for pasture is gocara, literally where the cow walks, the ground an animal knows and feeds on. And what is a monk's own pasture? The Buddha says it plainly: the four foundations of mindfulness. Body, feeling, mind, and mental qualities. That's home ground. Notice what this doesn't mean. It doesn't mean stay in your bubble, or never go out. The quail isn't safe because it hides. It's safe because it's somewhere it knows well, where it has cover. Out in the open, in somebody else's territory, scrolling and comparing and chasing, the hawk can dive. Back on familiar ground, with attention resting on the breath, the body, what's actually happening, the hawk can't get a grip. And the discourse goes on from here into a long story about kings, wheels and the whole human future, which we'll follow over the next two days. But it starts with a bird finding its way home.
screen: `THE QUAIL AND THE HAWK.` · `ISLANDS TO YOURSELVES.` · `GOCARA: WHERE THE COW WALKS.` · `HOME GROUND: THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PASTURE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and come back to your own ground. Feel the body sitting: that's one clod in the field. Feel the breath: another. Notice whether this moment is pleasant or not: another. When the mind wanders out into the open, into plans or worries or other people's lives, notice the hawk's shadow, and step back behind the clod. No drama. Just home again. The bell holds the time.
Your own pasture. In DN 26 the Buddha says: keep to your own ground, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the tempter gets no chance. Today's word.
Your line: your own pasture. Today, when you feel yourself drifting into a field that isn't yours, come back to one breath, one footstep, and stay on your own ground. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist meditation teachers often describe the four foundations of mindfulness as the practitioner's home ground, and the hawk-and-quail story is a familiar teaching picture in many Theravada communities.

slip behind a clod in your own field and call out.

original.note: Pali gocara: pasture, range, literally where the cow walks. in DN 26 it means the four foundations of mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'your own pasture' is about staying in your lane.
what it means: it's home ground for attention, the four foundations of mindfulness, where temptation gets no grip.
what a scholar hears: DN 26 opens with gocare bhikkhave caratha sake pettike visaye, and SN 47.6 (Sakunagghi) gives the hawk-and-quail parable for the same phrase.

notes: DN 26 and SN 47.6 paraphrased. Confirm the opening sequence in DN 26 (islands, then pasture, then 'Mara gets no chance') and the identification of pasture with the four satipatthanas.
Confirm SN 47.6 details: the quail caught out of its pettika visaya, the clods of a plowed field, the hawk striking the clod.
Islands/lamps (dipa) was discussed on y1 day 79; this day uses 'islands' for continuity with DN 26 translations.
